```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# the code runs only when ggplot2 (suggested, not required) is installed;
# figures use the cairo PNG device where it exists, since the Windows
# device can only store 256 colors and draws some states in gray
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4, dpi = 96,
                      dev.args = if (capabilities("cairo")) list(type = "cairo"),
                      eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE))
```

longCatEDA draws horizontal line plots of categorical longitudinal data:
each case is a horizontal line, time runs from left to right, and the
states are colors (Tueller, Van Dorn, & Bobashev, 2016). `plot()` draws
them with base graphics. When the
[ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org) package is installed, longCatEDA
also works with ggplot2, at three levels:

* `autoplot()` draws the complete plot as a `ggplot` object, to change
  with further layers, scales, and themes;
* `ggplot()` takes a `longCat` object as its data, and
  `scale_colour_longcat()` and `scale_fill_longcat()` give the colors of
  `plot()`, for plots of your own design;
* `sorter()`, `alignTime()`, and `patterns()` work on data in long format,
  one row per case and time, as used by ggplot2 and the tidyverse.

ggplot2 is suggested by longCatEDA, not required.

```{r packages}
library(longCatEDA)
library(ggplot2)
```

The examples use `example3`, 100 cases observed at 6 times in one of 5
states, here labeled as living situations.

```{r data}
labels <- c("Home", "School", "Work", "Jail", "Other")
lc <- longCat(example3, Labels = labels)
lc
```

## A complete plot: `autoplot()`

`autoplot()` draws the plot of `plot()`: the cases are sorted with
`sorter()` so that similar sequences are next to each other, and each case
is a line colored by its state.

```{r autoplot}
autoplot(lc)
```

The result is a `ggplot` object, so it can be changed like any other.
Groups from `sorter()` become facets, with the first group at the bottom
as in `plot()`; the colors come from `colChoose()`.

```{r autoplot-groups}
group <- rep(c("Treatment", "Control"), 50)
s <- sorter(lc, group = group)
autoplot(s, colScheme = "coldheat") +
  labs(title = "Living situation by study arm") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

For grayscale printing, line types tell the states apart.

```{r autoplot-lty}
autoplot(lc, colScheme = "gray", lty = c(1, 2), linewidth = 0.8)
```

### Events, time ranges, and alignment

`autoplot()` takes the options of `plot()` for events and times. Here two
events per case are added.

```{r events}
set.seed(45962)
events <- matrix(sample(1:3, 200, replace = TRUE), 100, 2)
event.times <- matrix(runif(200, 0, 6), 100, 2)
lce <- longCat(example3, Labels = labels, events = events,
               event.times = event.times,
               eventLabels = c("Arrest", "Drug test", "Hearing"))
autoplot(lce, which.events = 1)
```

`texclude` keeps the part of the plot between two times, and the
alignment options shift each case's times so that time 0 is the nth
occurrence of a state or event (see `alignTime()`). The cases are sorted
before the times are aligned, and `texclude` cuts the original times.

```{r align}
autoplot(lce, which.state = 4, nth.state = 1, events = FALSE,
         xlab = "Days since first jail stay") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2)
```

### Weighted data

With case weights (for example, survey weights), each case is a band with
a height proportional to its weight, and the y-axis label gives the
weighted N.

```{r weights}
set.seed(1)
lcw <- longCat(example3, Labels = labels, weights = rexp(100))
autoplot(lcw)
```

### Two variables

Given a second `longCat` object of the same cases, `autoplot()` draws the
two variables side by side, as facets of one plot, with the cases in the
same order: each case's row is the same in both panels. As in `plot(x, y)`,
`order = "joint"` sorts on both variables, and `y_args` sets the options
of the second panel.

```{r two-variables, fig.height = 5}
set.seed(3)
shifted <- example3 + matrix(sample(-1:1, 600, TRUE), 100)
use <- longCat(pmax(pmin(shifted, 5), 1),
               Labels = c("None", "Low", "Mid", "High", "Max"))
autoplot(s, use, y_args = list(colScheme = "topo"),
         titles = c("Living situation", "Drug use"))
```

## Your own plots: `ggplot()` and the color scales

`ggplot()` takes a `longCat` object as its data. The data are those of
`as.data.frame()`, one row per case and interval, with the cases sorted as
`plot()` sorts them and the vertical position of each case added:

* `row`: the plot row, counted from the bottom;
* `y`: the center of the case's line (or band);
* `ymin`, `ymax`: the edges of its band.

```{r fortify}
head(fortify(lc))
```

`scale_colour_longcat()` and `scale_fill_longcat()` color the states with
the schemes of `colChoose()`, as `plot()` does.

```{r own-segments}
ggplot(lc, aes(x = start, xend = stop, y = y, yend = y, colour = state)) +
  geom_segment(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_longcat("coldheat")
```

Bands work for weighted data too, and `fortify(x, what = "events")` gives
the events, placed on their case's band, for a layer of points.

```{r own-bands}
lcwe <- longCat(example3, Labels = labels, weights = rexp(100),
                events = events, event.times = event.times,
                eventLabels = c("Arrest", "Drug test", "Hearing"))
ggplot(lcwe) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = start, xmax = stop, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax,
                fill = state)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = time, y = y, shape = event),
             data = fortify(lcwe, what = "events")) +
  scale_fill_longcat() +
  labs(x = "Days", y = NULL)
```

## Long-format data

Data with one row per case and time can be sorted and aligned without
reshaping them. `sorter()` adds each case's plot row as the column `row`,
keeping every column and returning the rows in plot order. `group` names
a column with one value per case; ties are broken by case ID, so the
result does not depend on the order of the rows.

```{r long-sort}
set.seed(2)
long <- data.frame(pid = rep(sprintf("P%03d", 1:100), each = 6),
                   wave = rep(1:6, 100),
                   status = factor(labels[c(t(example3))], levels = labels),
                   site = rep(sample(c("North", "South"), 100, TRUE), each = 6))
d <- sorter(long, id = "pid", time = "wave", state = "status", group = "site")
head(d)
ggplot(d, aes(x = wave, xend = wave + 1, y = row, yend = row,
              colour = status)) +
  geom_segment(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_longcat(name = NULL) +
  facet_grid(site ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Wave", y = NULL)
```

With a `weight` column, `sorter()` also adds the band edges `ymin` and
`ymax`, as drawn by `plot()`. `alignTime()` adds aligned times, here the
waves since each person's first jail stay; `which.state` is a value of the
state column.

```{r long-align}
d <- alignTime(d, id = "pid", time = "wave", state = "status",
               which.state = "Jail", nth.state = 1)
ggplot(d, aes(x = aligned_time, xend = aligned_time + 1, y = row,
              yend = row, colour = status)) +
  geom_segment(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  scale_colour_longcat(name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Waves since first jail stay", y = NULL)
```

`as.data.frame()` turns a `longCat` object into long data, and
`as.longCat()` builds one from long data.

## Common patterns: `patterns()`

`patterns()` counts how many cases follow each sequence of states, with
repeated states collapsed into spells, from the most to the least common.
It works on `longCat` objects and on long data, with weights and groups.

```{r patterns}
p <- patterns(lc)
p
```

`autoplot()` (or `plot()`) draws the most common patterns, each as a row of
colored spells with its count and percent.

```{r patterns-plot}
autoplot(p, n = 8)
```

With groups, the patterns are counted, and drawn, within each group.

```{r patterns-groups, fig.height = 4.5}
autoplot(patterns(lc, by = group), n = 5, colScheme = "topo")
```

## Summary

| Task | Function |
|------|----------|
| A complete plot | `autoplot(lc)`, `autoplot(lc1, lc2)` |
| Data for your own plots | `ggplot(lc)`, `fortify(lc, what = "events")`, `as.data.frame(lc)` |
| The colors of `plot()` | `scale_colour_longcat()`, `scale_fill_longcat()` |
| Sort or align long data | `sorter(data, ...)`, `alignTime(data, ...)` |
| Most common sequences | `patterns()`, with `autoplot()` and `plot()` |

## Reference

Tueller, S. J., Van Dorn, R. A., & Bobashev, G. V. (2016). *Visualization
of categorical longitudinal and times series data* (Report No.
MR-0033-1602). Research Triangle Park, NC: RTI Press.
<https://doi.org/10.3768/rtipress.2016.mr.0033.1602>
